zero-to-one.lead: Peter Thiel's argument that real progress comes from creating something new — going from zero to one — instead of copying what already works.
zero-to-one.author: Peter Thiel
zero-to-one.notes:
## Notes

Competition is for losers. The goal is not to beat rivals at
their own game but to find a secret — something true that few
people agree with you on — and build a monopoly around it.

Thiel's four points stuck with me:

1. Proprietary technology — 10x better, not 10% better
2. Network effects — start small, dominate, then expand
3. Economies of scale — software wins here by default
4. Branding — real brands come from substance, not ads

The chapter on definite vs. indefinite optimism reframed how I
think about planning. A definite optimist has a plan and builds
toward it. An indefinite one keeps options open and ends up
owning nothing.
zero-to-one.highlights:
## Highlights

"What important truth do very few people agree with you on?"

"All happy companies are different: each one earns a monopoly
by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the
same: they failed to escape competition."

"The best startups might be considered slightly less extreme
kinds of cults."

"Monopoly is the condition of every successful business."

the-lean-startup.notes:
## Notes

Ries codified what good founders were already doing: build,
measure, learn — and do it fast. The MVP isn't a broken
product; it's the smallest experiment that tests your riskiest
assumption.

Validated learning beats vanity metrics. I still see teams
celebrating signups while retention flatlines. The book
gives you vocabulary to call that out without sounding
like a pessimist.

Pivot or persevere is a decision framework, not a vibe.
Set a threshold before you launch, then actually look at
the data when you hit it.

Some ideas aged poorly (innovation accounting can get
performative), but the core loop is still the best intro
to product experimentation I've found.
the-lean-startup.highlights:
## Highlights

"The goal of a startup is to figure out the right thing
to build — the thing customers want and will pay for —
as quickly as possible."

"We must learn what customers really want, not what they
say they want or what we think they should want."

"If we do not know who the customer is, we do not know
what quality is."

"The lesson of the MVP is that any additional work beyond
what was required to start learning is waste."

"Pivot or persevere — that is the question every startup
must answer."
the-lean-startup.author: Eric Ries
the-lean-startup.lead: Build-measure-learn — how constant iteration beats big launches.

essentialism.notes:
## Notes

The disciplined pursuit of less. The one-liner that
reorganized my calendar: if it isn't a clear yes, it's a
clear no. A 7-out-of-10 project is a 0 — the 90% rule
sounds brutal until you notice how much mediocre work you
were saying yes to out of politeness.

Trade-offs are real and pretending otherwise is how
agencies burn out. You can't do it all; the question is
never "how can I fit both" but "which problem do I want."
McKeown treats that as liberating rather than limiting,
and he's right.

The bit I actually implemented:

1. Build in buffers — estimate, then add 50%
2. Protect time to think; exploration is a job, not slack
3. Say no gracefully but say it — respect beats popularity
4. Remove obstacles instead of adding effort

Overlaps heavily with The ONE Thing, but this is the
better-written book. Where Keller gives you a question,
McKeown gives you a posture.
essentialism.highlights:
## Highlights

"If you don't prioritize your life, someone else will."

"The way of the Essentialist means living by design, not
by default."

"The word priority came into the English language in the
1400s. It was singular. It meant the very first or prior
thing. It stayed singular for the next five hundred
years."

"Essentialism is not about how to get more things done;
it's about how to get the right things done."

"We can either make our choices deliberately or allow
other people's agendas to control our lives."

"When we don't purposefully and deliberately choose where
to focus our energies and time, other people — our
bosses, our colleagues, our clients, and even our
families — will choose for us."
essentialism.author: Greg McKeown
essentialism.lead: The disciplined pursuit of less, but better.

the-intelligent-investor.notes:
## Notes

Mr. Market is the single best mental model in finance: a
manic business partner who offers you a different price
every day. You're free to ignore him. Price is what the
crowd feels; value is what the business earns. Most of
investing is refusing to let the first thing dictate the
second.

Margin of safety is the other pillar — buy with enough
room that being wrong doesn't ruin you. I apply it beyond
stocks now: project buffers, runway estimates, timeline
promises to clients. Assume your analysis is off and size
accordingly.

Graham's split between investor and speculator was
clarifying. An investor analyzes, insists on safety of
principal, and accepts adequate returns. Everything else —
including most of what fintech apps gamify — is
speculation wearing a suit.

Real talk: the chapters on railroad bonds are a slog and
the numbers are ancient. Read chapters 8 and 20, plus
Zweig's commentary, and you have 90% of the value.
the-intelligent-investor.highlights:
## Highlights

"The intelligent investor is a realist who sells to
optimists and buys from pessimists."

"In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in
the long run, it is a weighing machine."

"The investor's chief problem — and even his worst enemy —
is likely to be himself."

"An investment operation is one which, upon thorough
analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate
return. Operations not meeting these requirements are
speculative."

"Confronted with a challenge to distill the secret of
sound investment into three words, we venture the motto:
margin of safety."
the-intelligent-investor.author: Benjamin Graham
the-intelligent-investor.lead: The classic framework for value investing and margin of safety.

made-to-stick.notes:
## Notes

SUCCES: simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional,
stories. It's a checklist for why some ideas spread and
most die. I keep it taped next to every landing page and
pitch deck I review.

The curse of knowledge is the villain of the book, and
it's my job description. Once you know how the system
works, you physically cannot imagine not knowing it —
which is why engineers write docs nobody understands and
founders pitch features instead of outcomes.

Concrete beats abstract every time. "A man on the moon by
the end of the decade" is sticky; a mission statement
about "leveraging synergies" evaporates on contact. Most
copywriting fixes I make are just swapping abstractions
for something you can picture.

Finding the core means forced prioritization — if you say
three things, you say nothing. Same rule as good interface
design, which is probably why this book aged so well for
me.
made-to-stick.highlights:
## Highlights

"To strip an idea down to its core, we must be masters of
exclusion. We must relentlessly prioritize."

"The most basic way to get someone's attention is this:
Break a pattern."

"Once we know something, we find it hard to imagine what
it was like not to know it."

"Abstraction makes it harder to understand an idea and to
remember it. It also makes it harder to coordinate our
activities with others."

"If you say three things, you don't say anything."

"For an idea to stick, it's got to make the audience pay
attention, understand and remember it, agree and believe,
care, and be able to act on it."
made-to-stick.author: Chip Heath
made-to-stick.lead: Why some ideas survive and others die — the SUCCESs framework.

extreme-ownership.notes:
## Notes

The core idea survives the military packaging: everything
that happens on your watch is yours. When a release goes
sideways, the useful question isn't "who broke it" but
"what did I fail to communicate, check, or plan." Saying
that out loud as a lead changes the whole room's posture.

There are no bad teams, only bad leaders. The boat-crew
story — swap the leaders, watch the worst crew start
winning — is the best argument I know against blaming
"the talent" for process problems.

The rest of the toolkit, translated to product teams:

1. Believe in the mission or push back before you commit
2. Keep plans simple enough to survive contact with reality
3. Prioritize and execute — one fire at a time
4. Decentralized command: brief the intent, not the steps

The SEAL war stories run long and the corporate parallels
get repetitive by the back half. Skim those; keep the
framework.
extreme-ownership.highlights:
## Highlights

"Extreme Ownership. Leaders must own everything in their
world. There is no one else to blame."

"There are no bad teams, only bad leaders."

"Discipline equals freedom."

"It's not what you preach, it's what you tolerate."

"Relax, look around, make a call."

"If your team doesn't get it, you have not kept things
simple and you have failed."
extreme-ownership.author: Jocko Willink
extreme-ownership.lead: Leadership lessons from the battlefield, applied to teams and companies.

blitzscaling.notes:
## Notes

Blitzscaling means prioritizing speed over efficiency in
the face of uncertainty — deliberately doing inefficient
things because being first to scale matters more than
being right about the details. It's the opposite of almost
every other book on this shelf, which is exactly why it's
worth reading.

The growth-factor framing is the practical part: market
size, distribution, gross margins, and network effects on
one side; product/market fit and operational scalability
as the limiters. I run it as a checklist whenever a client
says "we want to scale."

Uncomfortable but true: at each stage — family, tribe,
village, city, nation — the company has to fire its old
processes. What got you to 10 people actively hurts at
100.

The caveat the fans skip: blitzscaling is for
winner-take-most markets with capital to burn. Most
companies I work with should not blitzscale, and to its
credit the book says so plainly.
blitzscaling.highlights:
## Highlights

"Blitzscaling is prioritizing speed over efficiency in
the face of uncertainty."

"The first mover advantage doesn't go to the first
company that launches, it goes to the first company that
scales."

"An entrepreneur is someone who jumps off a cliff and
builds a plane on the way down."

"If you're not embarrassed by the first version of your
product, you've shipped too late."

"In an era of blitzscaling, the risks of moving too slow
are often greater than the risks of moving too fast."
blitzscaling.author: Reid Hoffman
blitzscaling.lead: The lightning-fast path to building massively valuable companies.

the-e-myth-revisited.notes:
## Notes

The fatal assumption: because you understand the technical
work of a business, you understand the business of that
work. I've watched brilliant developers found agencies and
drown in exactly this. I've been the one drowning, too.

The three-personality split is the framework that stuck:

1. Technician — does the work, hates the paperwork
2. Manager — craves order, builds the systems
3. Entrepreneur — lives in the future, hates the present

Most founders are 70% technician, and the business pays
for it.

Work on your business, not just in it. The test: could
someone else run this from documentation alone? The
franchise-prototype lens sounds corporate, but for a small
studio it translates to playbooks, templates, and processes
that don't live in one person's head. Mine included.

The Sarah-and-her-pie-shop narrative device gets
saccharine. Push through — the operating manual underneath
is worth the cringe.
the-e-myth-revisited.highlights:
## Highlights

"If your business depends on you, you don't own a
business — you have a job."

"The fatal assumption is: if you understand the technical
work of a business, you understand a business that does
that technical work."

"The purpose of going into business is to get free of a
job so you can create jobs for other people."

"People who are exceptionally good in business aren't so
because of what they know but because of their insatiable
need to know more."

"Your business is nothing more than a distinct reflection
of who you are."
the-e-myth-revisited.author: Michael E. Gerber
the-e-myth-revisited.lead: Why most small businesses fail — and how to work on the business, not in it.

the-obstacle-is-the-way.notes:
## Notes

Stoicism packaged for people who won't read Marcus
Aurelius directly — which, honestly, was me. The frame is
three disciplines: perception, action, will. See things
plainly, act on what you control, endure what you can't.

The core move — the impediment to action advances action —
maps cleanly onto engineering work. A blocked API, a
budget cut, a dead-end design: each one narrows the
solution space, and the narrower space is usually where
the better idea was hiding.

Turning dead time into alive time changed how I handle
waiting — on client approvals, on deploys, on hiring. The
gap is where the prep happens, not where progress stops.

Style-wise it's anecdote, lesson, repeat, and some of the
history gets smoothed over to fit the thesis. But as a
pocket reference for bad weeks it earns its shelf space.
the-obstacle-is-the-way.highlights:
## Highlights

"The impediment to action advances action. What stands in
the way becomes the way."

"There is no good or bad without us, there is only
perception."

"The obstacle in the path becomes the path. Never forget,
within every obstacle is an opportunity to improve our
condition."

"Focus on the moment, not the monsters that may or may
not be up ahead."

"Problems are rarely as bad as we think — or rather, they
are precisely as bad as we think."

"You don't have to like something to master it — or to
use it to some advantage."
the-obstacle-is-the-way.author: Ryan Holiday
the-obstacle-is-the-way.lead: Stoic philosophy as a practical operating system for hard problems.

the-almanack-of-naval-ravikant.notes:
## Notes

Seek wealth, not money or status. Wealth is assets that
earn while you sleep. As someone who has billed a lot of
hours, that line stung — it's the whole argument for
building products and open source instead of only selling
time.

The leverage framework is the most useful model in the
book:

1. Labor and capital — old leverage, permissioned
2. Code and media — new leverage, permissionless
3. Zero marginal cost of replication is the unlock

Specific knowledge: the thing you can't be trained for,
that feels like play to you and looks like work to
everyone else. The design-engineering overlap is exactly
that for me — neither pure designers nor pure engineers
want to live there, so I do.

The happiness half is quieter but held up better than I
expected. Desire is a contract you make with yourself to
be unhappy until you get what you want. I reread that
chapter more than the wealth ones.
the-almanack-of-naval-ravikant.highlights:
## Highlights

"Seek wealth, not money or status. Wealth is having
assets that earn while you sleep."

"Earn with your mind, not your time."

"Specific knowledge is found by pursuing your genuine
curiosity and passion rather than whatever is hot right
now."

"Play long-term games with long-term people."

"Desire is a contract that you make with yourself to be
unhappy until you get what you want."

"A calm mind, a fit body, a house full of love. These
things cannot be bought — they must be earned."
the-almanack-of-naval-ravikant.author: Eric Jorgenson
the-almanack-of-naval-ravikant.lead: Wealth, happiness, and specific knowledge — distilled from Naval.

start-with-why.notes:
## Notes

The golden circle — why, how, what — is simple to the
point of obvious, yet most companies genuinely communicate
from the outside in. Look at any SaaS landing page:
features first, purpose nowhere. With the startups I work
with, flipping that order is often the whole positioning
fix.

People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it.
Overstated? Sure. But it explains why some brands get
evangelists and others get customers who churn at the
first price hike.

The law of diffusion section is the practical part: aim
early messaging at the innovators and early adopters who
buy on belief, not at the pragmatic majority who need
social proof you don't have yet.

Honest critique: it's a 20-minute TED talk stretched to
250 pages, and the Apple examples are cherry-picked. Read
it fast, keep the circle, move on.
start-with-why.highlights:
## Highlights

"People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it."

"There are only two ways to influence human behavior: you
can manipulate it or you can inspire it."

"Great companies don't hire skilled people and motivate
them, they hire already motivated people and inspire
them."

"Working hard for something we don't care about is called
stress; working hard for something we love is called
passion."

"The goal is not to do business with everybody who needs
what you have. The goal is to do business with people who
believe what you believe."
start-with-why.author: Simon Sinek
start-with-why.lead: People buy why you do it, not what you sell.

hooked.notes:
## Notes

The Hook Model is four steps: trigger, action, variable
reward, investment. Once you see the loop you can't unsee
it — every product I audit now gets mapped against it.

The variable reward chapter is the sharpest. Predictable
rewards get boring; slot-machine variability is what keeps
people pulling. It's also where the ethics get murky, and
Eyal only half-engages with that.

The investment step is underrated. Every bit of data,
content, or setup a user puts in makes the product harder
to leave. Good onboarding isn't about showing features —
it's about getting the user to invest early.

I use this two ways: to design honest habit loops for
products that deserve them, and to notice when an app is
running the loop on me. The manipulation matrix — would
you use it, does it materially improve lives — is a decent
gut check before you build any of this.
hooked.highlights:
## Highlights

"The technologies we use have turned into compulsions, if
not full-fledged addictions."

"Instead of relying on expensive marketing, habit-forming
companies link their services to the users' daily routines
and emotions."

"Variable rewards are one of the most powerful tools
companies implement to hook users."

"Emotions, particularly negative ones, are powerful
internal triggers and greatly influence our daily
routines."

"The enemy of forming new habits is past behaviors, and
research suggests that old habits die hard."
hooked.author: Nir Eyal
hooked.lead: How to build habit-forming products without dark patterns.

rework.notes:
## Notes

The most freeing idea in here: plans are guesses. Long-term
business plans are fantasy documents. Decide what you're
doing this week, ship it, adjust. I stopped writing
quarter-long specs after this book and nothing bad happened.

Embrace constraints. Less money, fewer people, less time —
constraints force you to build the small, sharp version of
the thing instead of the bloated one. Every side project
I've actually finished was scoped by a constraint.

Meetings are toxic and interruption is the enemy of
production. As a tech lead I default to async now and
guard long uninterrupted blocks for the team like they're
production infrastructure.

Workaholism isn't a badge. Code shipped at midnight creates
problems the well-rested version of you has to fix.

It reads like a stack of tweets, which is either the charm
or the flaw. For me: charm. You can re-read it in an hour
and it recalibrates you every time.
rework.highlights:
## Highlights

"Unless you're a fortune-teller, long-term business
planning is a fantasy."

"Workaholics aren't heroes. They don't save the day, they
just use it up. The real hero is already home because she
figured out a faster way to get things done."

"What you do is what matters, not what you think or say
or plan."

"Build half a product, not a half-assed product."

"Meetings are toxic."

"When you stand for something, decisions are obvious."
rework.author: Jason Fried
rework.lead: Ignore the real world, embrace constraints, and ship.

the-one-thing.notes:
## Notes

The focusing question is the whole book: what's the ONE
thing I can do such that by doing it everything else
becomes easier or unnecessary? I ask a version of it at
the start of every sprint now, and it embarrasses most
of my to-do lists.

The domino metaphor stuck. Line up priorities so knocking
over one small thing sets up the next, bigger one. Most
roadmaps I see are flat lists — no sequencing, no leverage.

What I actually changed after reading it:

1. Time-block the ONE thing first, protect it ruthlessly
2. Stop pretending multitasking works — switching is a tax
3. Break big goals down until "someday" becomes "right now"
4. Treat willpower as a battery and schedule around it

Fair warning: it's one idea stretched to book length. You
could read the first third and stop. The idea is good
enough that I didn't mind.
the-one-thing.highlights:
## Highlights

"What's the ONE Thing you can do such that by doing it
everything else will be easier or unnecessary?"

"Success is sequential, not simultaneous."

"Extraordinary results are directly determined by how
narrow you can make your focus."

"Multitasking is merely the opportunity to screw up more
than one thing at a time."

"Work is a rubber ball. If you drop it, it will bounce
back. The other four balls — family, health, friends,
integrity — are made of glass."
the-one-thing.author: Gary Keller
the-one-thing.lead: Extraordinary results come from narrowing focus to one thing at a time.

ego-is-the-enemy.notes:
## Notes

Holiday's thesis: ego is the voice that rewrites history
to make you the hero, blocks feedback, and turns success
into the thing that ruins you. Ambition is fine;
entitlement is poison.

The three-part structure — Aspire, Success, Failure —
mirrors a career arc. The Success section hit hardest:
that's the phase where people stop learning because they
think they've made it.

The canvas strategy stuck with me: find canvases for other
people to paint on. Early on, making your boss and peers
better is the fastest way to become someone worth betting
on. Ego calls that beneath you; it isn't.

Talk is the other trap. Announcing plans feels like
progress and quietly replaces it. I've shipped more since
I started keeping projects quiet until they're real.

Some repetition if you've read his other Stoic books, but
it works as a pre-mortem before any launch or promotion.
ego-is-the-enemy.highlights:
## Highlights

"Ego is the enemy of what you want and of what you have."

"Talk depletes us. Talking and doing fight for the same
resources."

"Impressing people is utterly different from being truly
impressive."

"Passion typically masks a weakness."

"Be lesser, do more."
ego-is-the-enemy.author: Ryan Holiday
ego-is-the-enemy.lead: Humility and discipline beat ego in every season of life.

never-split-the-difference.notes:
## Notes

Voss's premise: negotiation is emotional, not rational, so
stop bargaining like an economist. Tactical empathy — make
the other side feel understood before you steer — beats
splitting the difference every time.

The tools I actually use on client calls:

1. Mirroring — repeat their last three words, then wait
2. Labeling — "it seems like budget is the real worry"
3. Calibrated questions — "how am I supposed to do that?"
4. The late-night FM DJ voice when things get tense

Getting to "no" was the reframe for me. People feel safe
saying no, so ask questions where no is progress: "is now
a bad time?" opens more doors than chasing a hollow yes.

Yes is nothing without how. I stopped celebrating verbal
agreement and started asking implementation questions
until the deal was real. Fewer ghosted proposals since.
never-split-the-difference.highlights:
## Highlights

"He who has learned to disagree without being disagreeable
has discovered the most valuable secret of negotiation."

"Negotiate in their world. Persuasion is not about how
bright or smooth or forceful you are. It's about the other
party convincing themselves that the solution you want is
their own idea."

"'No' is the start of the negotiation, not the end of it."

"The most dangerous negotiation is the one you don't know
you're in."

"Yes is nothing without How."

"Negotiation is not an act of battle; it's a process of
discovery."
never-split-the-difference.author: Chris Voss
never-split-the-difference.lead: Negotiation tactics from an FBI hostage negotiator.

trillion-dollar-coach.notes:
## Notes

Bill Campbell coached Steve Jobs, Larry Page, and Eric
Schmidt at the same time and never took a dollar for it.
This book is Google's attempt to write down his playbook
before it disappeared with him.

The core move: work the team, not the problem. When
something breaks, Campbell didn't debug the issue, he
debugged the people — who stopped talking to whom, whose
trust got dented. Fix that and the issue fixes itself.

Care personally, challenge directly. He'd hug you and then
tell you exactly what you were screwing up. The warmth is
what bought him the license to be blunt.

Only coach the coachable — honesty and humility are
prerequisites, not outcomes. That one sentence has saved
me from a couple of doomed engagements.

It's hagiography by design, written by people who loved
him. Extract the habits, skip the cult of Bill.
trillion-dollar-coach.highlights:
## Highlights

"The top priority of any manager is the well-being and
success of her people."

"Only coach the coachable."

"To care about people you have to care about people."

"If you're a great manager, your people will make you a
leader. They acclaim that, not you."

"Leadership is about service to something that is bigger
than you: your company, your team."
trillion-dollar-coach.author: Eric Schmidt
trillion-dollar-coach.lead: Leadership lessons from Bill Campbell, coach to Silicon Valley legends.

super-pumped.notes:
## Notes

Isaac's Uber book is really a portrait of Travis Kalanick
— relentless, abrasive, willing to break rules until the
rules pushed back. It's the definitive case study of
growth-at-all-costs culture and the bill coming due.

The Greyball chapters are uncomfortable reading for anyone
who builds "move fast" products. Evading regulators with
software wasn't a bug in the culture; it was the culture,
codified and shipped.

What stuck: the values on Uber's wall — "always be
hustlin'," "toe-stepping" — weren't decoration. People
optimized for exactly what leadership rewarded. Culture is
the incentive structure, not the poster.

The 2017 collapse reads like dominoes: Susan Fowler's blog
post, the Greyball exposé, the Waymo lawsuit, the board
coup. Each one survivable alone. Together, fatal.

Founder-friendly governance made Kalanick nearly
impossible to remove even after all that. Worth
remembering when everyone praises founder control.
super-pumped.highlights:
## Highlights

"Travis needed Uber, maybe even more than Uber needed
Travis."

"Uber was Travis. Travis was Uber."

"Better to ask forgiveness than permission."

"Kalanick had baked his personality into the company's
fourteen core values."

"For Kalanick, winning wasn't just a goal. It was a way of
life."
super-pumped.author: Mike Isaac
super-pumped.lead: The rise and fall of Uber — ambition, speed, and consequences.

remote.notes:
## Notes

Fried and DHH wrote this in 2013 and the pandemic made it
look prophetic. The core argument still holds: the office
is a place people go to get interrupted, and real work
happens in long uninterrupted stretches.

The trust point is the one managers keep dodging. If you
need to watch people work, you have a hiring problem, not
a location problem. Remote just exposes it.

Running a distributed studio, the practices that stuck:

1. Async by default — write it down, decide in threads
2. Overlap hours — a few shared hours beat full calendars
3. Judge output, not presence — the work is the evidence
4. Hire everywhere — local-only hiring shrinks your pool

It's a manifesto, so it oversells. Some work really is
better in a room. But the burden of proof flipped, and
this book flipped it early.
remote.highlights:
## Highlights

"The office during the day has become the last place
people want to be when they really want to get work done."

"If we're struggling with trust issues, it means we made a
poor hiring decision."

"As an employer, restricting your hiring to a small
geographic region means you're not getting the best people
you can."

"When you can't see someone all day long, the only thing
you have to evaluate is the work."

"The new luxury is the luxury of freedom and time. Once
you've had a taste of that life, no corner office or fancy
chef will be able to drag you back."
remote.author: Jason Fried
remote.lead: Office not required — building a calm company that works from anywhere.

chaos-monkeys.notes:
## Notes

The most cynical book about Silicon Valley I've read, and
probably the most honest. Martinez goes from Goldman to a
YC startup to selling ads at Facebook, burning every
bridge in print on the way out.

The adtech chapters are genuinely educational. If you want
to understand how targeting, auctions, and identity
matching actually work under the hood of the ad economy,
this beats most textbooks.

His line about investors, employees, and entrepreneurs is
the cleanest model of startup power dynamics I know. Once
you see who has money and who has time, every negotiation
suddenly makes sense.

Take the swagger with a grain of salt — he's the hero of
every anecdote — but the mechanics of acquihires, vesting,
and term sheets are real, and nobody else writes about
them this plainly.
chaos-monkeys.highlights:
## Highlights

"Investors are people with more money than time. Employees
are people with more time than money. Entrepreneurs are
simply the seductive go-betweens."

"Startups are business experiments performed with other
people's money."

"The best minds of my generation are thinking about how to
make people click ads."

"Facebook is full of true believers who really, really,
really are not doing it for the money."
chaos-monkeys.author: Antonio Garcia Martinez
chaos-monkeys.lead: A memoir of Facebook ads, startups, and Silicon Valley excess.

the-power-law.notes:
## Notes

Mallaby's history of venture capital lands one statistical
point and never lets go: returns follow a power law. Most
bets lose, and everything gets paid for by one or two
outliers. Once you accept that, the weird behavior of VCs
starts looking rational.

The corollary changed how I read term sheets: a fund's
downside is capped at 1x while the upside is unbounded, so
the only fatal mistake is missing the outlier. Passing on
Airbnb costs more than backing ten duds.

Great chapters on the lineage — Arthur Rock freeing the
Traitorous Eight, Don Valentine betting on markets over
founders, YC industrializing the seed round. The craft got
passed hand to hand like a guild secret.

The SoftBank/WeWork ending is the cautionary tale: capital
as a weapon works right up until the power law reminds you
that valuation isn't value.

Useful reading if you build for VC-backed startups. It
explains why your clients behave the way they do.
the-power-law.highlights:
## Highlights

"Venture capital is not even a home-run business. It's a
grand-slam business."

"The best investment in a successful fund equals or
outperforms the entire rest of the fund combined."

"I like opportunities that are addressing markets so big
that even the management team can't get in its way."

"I believe so strongly in people that I think talking to
the individual is much more important than finding out too
much about what they want to do."

"The reasonable man adapts himself to the world: the
unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to
himself. Therefore all progress depends on the
unreasonable man."
the-power-law.author: Sebastian Mallaby
the-power-law.lead: Venture capital and the making of the new economy.

small-giants.notes:
## Notes

The premise is quietly radical: growth is a choice, not a
law of nature. Burlingham profiles fourteen companies that
had every chance to scale — Anchor Brewing, Zingerman's,
Clif Bar — and deliberately stayed small to stay great.

The pattern across all of them: ownership stays inside the
company. The moment outside capital shows up, someone else
gets a vote on what success means, and the default vote is
always "bigger."

Mojo is his word for what these companies have — the thing
you feel walking in the door. It comes from intimacy: with
the community, with customers, with employees. Intimacy
doesn't scale, which is exactly the point.

As someone who runs a small studio on purpose, this book
felt like permission. The interesting question isn't "how
big can this get" but "what is this for."
small-giants.highlights:
## Highlights

"They were utterly determined to be the best at what they
did. Being the best was, in fact, how most of them defined
success."

"I was thrilled at the notion that you could have a small,
prestigious, profitable business, and that it would be all
right."

"They had all faced the choice of whether to grow as fast
and as big as possible, and they had all decided against
it."

"There is a great deal to be said for having a business
you can wrap your arms around."
small-giants.author: Bo Burlingham
small-giants.lead: Companies that choose to be great instead of big.

how-google-works.notes:
## Notes

The useful idea is "smart creatives" — people who combine
technical depth, business sense, and creative flair — and
the claim that management's only real job is building a
place where they can thrive at scale.

Culture is set early and then it's set. Schmidt and
Rosenberg argue you write down your values while the team
is small, hire against them ruthlessly, and never delegate
hiring. Committees over hiring managers was the spiciest
take, and I've come around to it.

Ship and iterate over polish and launch. Base plans on
technical insight, not market research. Both sound obvious
until you watch a roadmap get built entirely out of
competitor screenshots.

It's dated in places — the Google described here doesn't
quite exist anymore — but as a snapshot of how a platform
era company thought about talent, it holds up.
how-google-works.highlights:
## Highlights

"If you focus on your competition, you will never deliver
anything truly innovative."

"Your title makes you a manager. Your people make you a
leader."

"The only way for businesses to consistently succeed is to
attract smart creative employees and create an environment
where they can thrive at scale."

"Ideas come from anywhere."

"For a manager, the right answer to the question 'What is
the single most important thing you do at work?' is
hiring."
how-google-works.author: Eric Schmidt
how-google-works.lead: How Google thinks about strategy, culture, and decision-making.

the-psychology-of-money.notes:
## Notes

The thesis fits in one sentence: doing well with money is
about behavior, not intelligence. Nobody is crazy — we all
price risk based on the slice of history we happened to
live through.

Wealth is what you don't see. The cars not bought, the
upgrades skipped. Rich is visible income; wealth is the
invisible option to do what you want later. Confusing the
two is how high earners stay broke.

The chapters I keep quoting to founder friends:

1. Tails drive everything — a few bets pay for the rest
2. Enough — the moving goalpost is what ruins people
3. Room for error — plan on the plan not going to plan
4. Reasonable beats rational — pick what you'll stick with

Housel's own portfolio is boring on purpose: a house,
index funds, cash. Coming from a finance writer, that
restraint is the most convincing argument in the book.
the-psychology-of-money.highlights:
## Highlights

"Doing well with money has a little to do with how smart
you are and a lot to do with how you behave."

"Wealth is what you don't see."

"The hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to
stop moving."

"Controlling your time is the highest dividend money
pays."

"Spending money to show people how much money you have is
the fastest way to have less money."

"Save. Just save. You don't need a specific reason to
save."
the-psychology-of-money.author: Morgan Housel
the-psychology-of-money.lead: Behavior beats intelligence when it comes to money.

the-signal-and-the-noise.notes:
## Notes

Silver's core point: we don't have an information problem,
we have a prediction problem. More data mostly means more
noise, and confident people mistake the noise for signal.

The fox vs. hedgehog split maps cleanly onto product work.
Hedgehogs have one big idea and force everything through
it; foxes hold many small ideas loosely and keep updating.
Foxes forecast better. So do good tech leads.

Think in probabilities, not verdicts. The Bayesian habit —
state a prior, weigh new evidence, revise — is the whole
book in one move. Saying "70% confident" and meaning it
beats sounding certain.

Weather forecasting is the quiet hero chapter. It improved
for decades because forecasts got scored against reality
every single day. Most teams never close that loop on
their own predictions, which is why they never improve.

Overfitting stuck with me as a design lesson too: a model
that explains the past perfectly usually says the least
about the future.
the-signal-and-the-noise.highlights:
## Highlights

"The signal is the truth. The noise is what distracts us
from the truth."

"We need to stop, and admit it: we have a prediction
problem. We love to predict things — and we aren't very
good at it."

"The most calamitous failures of prediction usually have a
lot in common. We focus on those signals that tell a story
about the world as we would like it to be, not how it
really is."

"The instinctual shortcut that we take when we have 'too
much information' is to engage with it selectively,
picking out the parts we like and ignoring the remainder."

"Big Data will produce progress — eventually. How quickly
it does, and whether we regress in the meantime, will
depend on us."
the-signal-and-the-noise.author: Nate Silver
the-signal-and-the-noise.lead: Why most predictions fail — and some do not.

the-tao-of-charlie-munger.notes:
## Notes

This is a quote book — one Munger line per page with
Clark's commentary underneath. The commentary is thin, but
as a Munger sampler it earns its spot on the shelf.

The recurring theme is temperament over intellect. Munger
keeps saying the returns go to people who can sit still,
avoid envy, and not do anything dumb while everyone around
them is busy being clever.

Read back to back with Griffin's book, the overlap is big.
If you only read one, read Griffin. This one works better
as something you flip open at random before a hard call.

What I keep coming back to: envy is the dumbest sin
because it's the only one you can't have any fun at. That
reframe kills a lot of comparison anxiety in startup land.

Also a reminder that reading is the job. Munger claims he
has never known a wise person who didn't read constantly.
Neither have I.
the-tao-of-charlie-munger.highlights:
## Highlights

"In my whole life, I have known no wise people who didn't
read all the time — none, zero."

"It's waiting that helps you as an investor, and a lot of
people just can't stand to wait."

"Envy is a really stupid sin because it's the only one you
could never possibly have any fun at."

"Spend each day trying to be a little wiser than you were
when you woke up."

"There is no better teacher than history in determining
the future."
the-tao-of-charlie-munger.author: David Clark
the-tao-of-charlie-munger.lead: Wit and wisdom from Berkshire Hathaway's vice chairman.

charlie-munger.notes:
## Notes

Griffin distills Munger into one move: build a latticework
of mental models from many disciplines and run every big
decision through several of them at once. One model is a
hammer, and everything starts looking like a nail.

Circle of competence is the one I use weekly. Knowing the
edge of what you actually understand matters more than how
big the circle is. Most bad calls I've watched happen came
from someone quietly stepping outside theirs.

The models that stuck:

1. Inversion — ask what guarantees failure, avoid that
2. Incentives — never ignore what people are paid to do
3. Margin of safety — leave room to be wrong
4. Social proof — crowds are a signal, not an argument

The real discipline is mostly about not doing things. Sit
on your hands until the odds are heavily in your favor,
then act big. That patience is harder than any analysis.
charlie-munger.highlights:
## Highlights

"Take a simple idea and take it seriously."

"Knowing what you don't know is more useful than being
brilliant."

"It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like
us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid,
instead of trying to be very intelligent."

"The big money is not in the buying and selling, but in
the waiting."

"Invert, always invert."

"A great business at a fair price is superior to a fair
business at a great price."
charlie-munger.author: Tren Griffin
charlie-munger.lead: Mental models and multidisciplinary thinking from Charlie Munger.

the-daily-stoic.notes:
## Notes

One page per day, one idea per page. It's a delivery system
for Marcus Aurelius and Seneca without requiring you to
parse 2,000-year-old sentence structure before coffee.

The recurring theme: control what you can, release what you
can't, and stop adding drama to events that are already
neutral. That maps cleanly onto client work, launches, and
anything involving other humans.

I don't read it daily anymore, but I keep it on the desk for
weeks when everything feels reactive. The format lowers the
activation energy.

Holiday repackages ancient philosophy for modern
professionals. Some purists roll their eyes; I care whether
it helps me show up better on Tuesday.
the-daily-stoic.highlights:
## Highlights

"You have power over your mind — not outside events.
Realize this, and you will find strength."

"The impediment to action advances action. What stands in
the way becomes the way."

"We suffer more often in imagination than in reality."

"It is not the man who has too little, but the man who
craves more, that is poor."

"Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should
be. Be one."
the-daily-stoic.author: Ryan Holiday
the-daily-stoic.lead: 366 meditations on wisdom, perseverance, and the good life.

freakonomics.notes:
## Notes

Incentives explain almost everything, and they're usually
not the incentives on the org chart. The sumo wrestlers
and the cheating teachers both respond perfectly to the
system they're actually in, not the one on paper. Every
product metric I've ever set has had a sumo problem
hiding in it somewhere.

Information asymmetry is the other big hammer. Real estate
agents leave their own houses on the market longer than
their clients' — they capture the upside of waiting, you
don't. Whenever an expert's advice and their commission
point the same way, be suspicious.

Correlation vs. causation is the chapter I wish every
stakeholder had read. More police and less crime can both
be caused by a third thing. Dashboards make this mistake
at scale every day.

The abortion-crime chapter is the famous one and the
shakiest — the methods took real criticism afterwards.
Good reminder that clever beats careful only until
someone checks the math.
freakonomics.highlights:
## Highlights

"Incentives are the cornerstone of modern life."

"Morality, it could be argued, represents the way that
people would like the world to work, whereas economics
represents how it actually does work."

"An incentive is a bullet, a lever, a key: an often tiny
object with astonishing power to change a situation."

"Information is a beacon, a cudgel, an olive branch, a
deterrent — all depending on who wields it and how."

"Knowing what to measure and how to measure it makes a
complicated world much less so."
freakonomics.author: Steven D. Levitt
freakonomics.lead: The hidden side of everything — incentives explain more than you think.

the-dip.notes:
## Notes

Quitting isn't the opposite of grit — it's how you fund
it. Godin's argument: strategic quitters dump dead ends
fast so they have the resources to push through the one
dip that's actually worth crossing.

The three curves are a useful diagnostic for any project
on my plate:

1. The Dip — hard middle, big payoff if you push through
2. The Cul-de-Sac — flat forever, quit now
3. The Cliff — feels fine until it suddenly doesn't

The rule I took away: decide your quitting conditions
before you start, in writing. Quitting in the middle of
the dip is the worst outcome — you pay the cost and skip
the reward.

Being best in the world sounds grandiose until you notice
the world part is up to you. Best design studio for
early-stage fintech in your region is a winnable market.
Best design studio is not.

It's a 96-page blog post, honestly. But I've reread it
before every quit-or-double-down decision since.
the-dip.highlights:
## Highlights

"Never quit something with great long-term potential just
because you can't deal with the stress of the moment."

"Being the best in the world is seriously underrated."

"Winners quit fast, quit often, and quit without guilt —
until they commit to beating the right Dip for the right
reasons."

"Extraordinary benefits accrue to the tiny minority of
people who are able to push just a tiny bit longer than
most."

"Quit the wrong stuff. Stick with the right stuff. Have
the guts to do one or the other."
the-dip.author: Seth Godin
the-dip.lead: The low point every worthwhile pursuit hits — and when to quit or push through.

titan.notes:
## Notes

Rockefeller's edge wasn't vision, it was accounting. He
knew the cost of every barrel, hoop, and rail rebate when
his competitors were guessing. Boring operational rigor,
compounded over decades, beat every flashier rival.

Standard Oil is the original playbook for economies of
scale: own the barrel factories, the pipelines, the tank
cars. Every acquisition made the next one cheaper. It's
the same logic platform companies run today, minus the
antitrust ending.

The ledger habit stuck with me. He recorded every personal
expense from age sixteen in Ledger A and audited himself
like a business. Measurement as self-discipline, a century
before dashboards.

Chernow doesn't sand off the contradictions: ruthless
monopolist, devout Baptist, and the biggest philanthropist
of his era, all the same man. The book refuses to resolve
it, which is why it works.

At 832 pages it's a commitment. Worth it — but read it as
history, not as a how-to.
titan.highlights:
## Highlights

"Success comes from keeping the ears open and the mouth
closed."

"Do not many of us who fail to achieve big things fail
because we lack concentration — the art of concentrating
the mind on the thing to be done at the proper time and
to the exclusion of everything else?"

"I do not think there is any other quality so essential
to success of any kind as the quality of perseverance."

"Singleness of purpose is one of the chief essentials for
success in life, no matter what may be one's aim."

"Don't be afraid to give up the good to go for the
great."
titan.author: Ron Chernow
titan.lead: The definitive biography of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.

leonardo-da-vinci.notes:
## Notes

The notebooks are the real subject. Seven thousand pages
of to-do lists like describe the tongue of the woodpecker —
curiosity with zero regard for usefulness. Isaacson's
point: that indiscriminate curiosity is exactly what fed
the art. The engineering made the painting better, and
vice versa.

Leonardo shipped almost nothing. He carried the Mona Lisa
around for sixteen years, still tweaking it. Isaacson
treats this generously; I read it as a warning. Genius
plus no deadline equals a garage full of unfinished
prototypes.

He was a designer before the word existed: obsessive about
observation, prototyping, and how things actually work
under the surface. The anatomy dissections just to paint a
smile correctly — that's user research taken to its
logical extreme.

Best takeaway for anyone in a creative field: skills
compound across disciplines. Leonardo's optics fed his
painting, his stagecraft fed his engineering. Being
T-shaped is fine; he argues for being comb-shaped.
leonardo-da-vinci.highlights:
## Highlights

"Talent hits a target no one else can hit; genius hits a
target no one else can see."

"Vision without execution is hallucination."

"Learning never exhausts the mind."

"The greatest geniuses sometimes accomplish more when
they work less."

"Obstacles do not bend me. Every obstacle yields to stern
resolve."
leonardo-da-vinci.author: Walter Isaacson
leonardo-da-vinci.lead: An restless mind that connected art, science, and observation.

the-war-of-art.notes:
## Notes

Naming the enemy is half the book's value. Resistance is
whatever stops you from sitting down and doing the work —
and it shows up as procrastination, research, perfectionism,
even busywork that looks productive. I recognize all of
mine now.

The fear compass is the sharpest idea: the more a project
scares you, the more it matters. Resistance is strongest
exactly where the work is most important. I check this
before dropping a side project — is it boring, or is it
scary?

Turning pro is a decision, not a milestone. The pro shows
up every day, works whether inspired or not, and doesn't
take failure or success personally. Amateurs wait to feel
ready.

The muse mysticism in part three isn't for me, but it's
short. The first hundred pages are the ones I reread every
time a project stalls.
the-war-of-art.highlights:
## Highlights

"The more scared we are of a work or calling, the more
sure we can be that we have to do it."

"Are you paralyzed with fear? That's a good sign."

"Resistance is experienced as fear; the degree of fear
equates to the strength of Resistance."

"The most important thing about art is to work. Nothing
else matters except sitting down every day and trying."

"The amateur plays for fun. The professional plays for
keeps."

"Rule of thumb: The more important a call or action is to
our soul's evolution, the more Resistance we will feel
toward pursuing it."
the-war-of-art.author: Steven Pressfield
the-war-of-art.lead: Resistance is the enemy of creative work — and how to beat it.

so-good-they-can-x27-t-ignore-you.notes:
## Notes

Follow your passion is terrible advice, and Newport
actually shows the work behind that claim. Passion is not
a preexisting thing you discover; it's a byproduct of
getting good at something rare and valuable.

Career capital is the frame I use with junior designers
now. Autonomy, mission, creative freedom — all the things
people want from work — are bought with skill. Demand them
before you've earned them and the market says no.

The craftsman mindset flips the question from what can
this job offer me to what can I offer this job. Ten years
into client work, the people I see plateau are the ones
still asking the first question.

His control traps are real. I hit the first one going
freelance too early — chasing autonomy without the capital
to back it up. The book would have saved me a rough year.
so-good-they-can-x27-t-ignore-you.highlights:
## Highlights

"Be so good they can't ignore you."

"Passion comes after you put in the hard work to become
excellent at something valuable, not before."

"The craftsman mindset focuses on what you can offer the
world, the passion mindset focuses instead on what the
world can offer you."

"Working right trumps finding the right work."

"If you want to love what you do, abandon the passion
mindset (what can the world offer me?) and instead adopt
the craftsman mindset (what can I offer the world?)."
so-good-they-can-x27-t-ignore-you.lead: Why skills trump passion in the quest for work you love.
so-good-they-can-x27-t-ignore-you.author: Cal Newport

the-richest-man-in-babylon.notes:
## Notes

The whole book is one rule wearing different togas: pay
yourself first. A tenth of everything you earn is yours to
keep, before rent, before anything. A century of personal
finance writing is basically footnotes to this.

What stuck from the parables:

1. Make your savings work — idle gold earns nothing
2. Guard principal — chasing returns you don't
   understand is how you lose it
3. Take advice only from people who practice the craft,
   not from the brickmaker on jewels
4. Increase your ability to earn — skill is the real
   compounding asset

As a freelancer-turned-studio-owner, the tenth-of-income
rule works better than any budgeting app I've tried. It's
dumb, it's automatic, and it survives bad months.

The fake old-timey prose grates after a while, but the
book is 124 pages. You can forgive a lot at that length.
the-richest-man-in-babylon.highlights:
## Highlights

"A part of all you earn is yours to keep."

"Wealth, like a tree, grows from a tiny seed."

"Advice is one thing that is freely given away, but watch
that you take only what is worth having."

"Opportunity is a haughty goddess who wastes no time with
those who are unprepared."

"Better a little caution than a great regret."

"Where the determination is, the way can be found."
the-richest-man-in-babylon.author: George S. Clason
the-richest-man-in-babylon.lead: Timeless parables about saving, investing, and building wealth.

outliers.notes:
## Notes

The self-made genius is mostly a story we tell after the
fact. Gladwell keeps showing the hidden scaffolding: Bill
Gates got unlimited terminal time in 1968, the Beatles got
Hamburg, Canadian hockey stars got born in January.

The 10,000 hours number gets quoted badly. The real point
isn't the count — it's that mastery needs an opportunity
structure that lets you put the hours in at all. Talent
without access goes nowhere.

The cockpit chapters are the best part. Korean Air didn't
fix its crash record with better pilots; it fixed the
communication culture so first officers could challenge
captains. Team dynamics beat individual skill.

Meaningful work needs three things — autonomy, complexity,
and a connection between effort and reward. That's a
better checklist for evaluating a job offer than any
salary band.

Gladwell cherry-picks, and the 10k-hour research has taken
real hits since. Read it as a lens, not as law.
outliers.highlights:
## Highlights

"Practice isn't the thing you do once you're good. It's
the thing you do that makes you good."

"No one — not rock stars, not professional athletes, not
software billionaires, and not even geniuses — ever makes
it alone."

"It's not how much money we make that ultimately makes us
happy between nine and five. It's whether or not our work
fulfills us."

"Success is not a random act. It arises out of a
predictable and powerful set of circumstances and
opportunities."

"Who we are cannot be separated from where we're from."
outliers.author: Malcolm Gladwell
outliers.lead: Success is not just talent — context, culture, and timing matter enormously.

no-rules-rules.notes:
## Notes

Talent density is the whole trick. Every other Netflix
policy — no vacation limits, no expense approvals, no
KPIs — only works because they pay top of market and cut
adequate performers. Copy the freedom without the density
and you get chaos.

Lead with context, not control. This is the line I quote
most to founders. If you have to approve every decision,
you either hired wrong or you're hoarding information your
team needs to decide well.

The keeper test is uncomfortable and useful: if this
person quit tomorrow, would I fight to keep them? Asking
it honestly about a team surfaces problems everyone
already knows about but nobody names.

The candor chapters travel less well than the book admits.
Erin Meyer's culture-mapping sections are the honest part:
what reads as directness in Amsterdam reads as an insult
in Tokyo.
no-rules-rules.highlights:
## Highlights

"Lead with context, not control."

"Adequate performance gets a generous severance
package."

"A fast and innovative workplace is made up of what we
call stunning colleagues — highly talented people, of
diverse backgrounds and perspectives, who are
exceptionally creative, accomplish significant amounts of
important work, and collaborate effectively."

"Only say about someone what you will say to their
face."

"If a person on your team were to quit tomorrow, would
you try to change their mind? Or would you accept their
resignation, perhaps with a little relief?"
no-rules-rules.author: Reed Hastings
no-rules-rules.lead: Netflix culture — freedom and responsibility at scale.

ogilvy-on-advertising.notes:
## Notes

Advertising is salesmanship, not art. Ogilvy hammers this
on nearly every page, and it maps straight onto design
work: a landing page that wins awards but doesn't convert
is a failure, full stop.

The headline math changed how I budget my effort. Five
times as many people read the headline as the body, so the
headline deserves five times the iterations. Same logic
applies to hero sections and app store screenshots.

His rules that still hold in 2026:

1. Do the homework — research before creative
2. One big idea, or the ad sails past unnoticed
3. Long copy sells, if every line earns its keep
4. Respect the reader's intelligence

Some chapters are pure 1980s Madison Avenue time capsule.
Read it for the principles, not the tactics.
ogilvy-on-advertising.highlights:
## Highlights

"If it doesn't sell, it isn't creative."

"I do not regard advertising as entertainment or an art
form, but as a medium of information."

"On the average, five times as many people read the
headline as read the body copy. When you have written
your headline, you have spent eighty cents out of your
dollar."

"Unless your advertising contains a big idea, it will
pass like a ship in the night."

"The consumer isn't a moron; she is your wife."

"Never write an advertisement which you wouldn't want
your family to read."
ogilvy-on-advertising.author: David Ogilvy
ogilvy-on-advertising.lead: I do not regard advertising as entertainment or an art form, but as a medium of information.

deep-work.notes:
## Notes

The core claim: the ability to focus without distraction is
getting rarer at exactly the moment it's getting more
valuable. For anyone who builds things, that's the whole
business case for protecting your calendar.

Deep work is a skill, not a mood. You train it like a
muscle, and every glance at Slack detrains it. Attention
residue explains why a quick check between tasks quietly
costs me half an hour of real thinking.

Newport's four scheduling philosophies:

1. Monastic — disappear completely
2. Bimodal — long stretches on, long stretches off
3. Rhythmic — same deep block every day
4. Journalistic — switch on whenever you can

Rhythmic is the only one that survives client work. Deep
block in the morning, meetings pushed to the afternoon,
phone in another room.
deep-work.highlights:
## Highlights

"The ability to perform deep work is becoming
increasingly rare at exactly the same time it is becoming
increasingly valuable in our economy."

"Clarity about what matters provides clarity about what
does not."

"If you don't produce, you won't thrive — no matter how
skilled or talented you are."

"Who you are, what you think, feel, and do, what you
love — is the sum of what you focus on."

"A deep life is a good life."
deep-work.author: Cal Newport
deep-work.lead: Focused work without distraction is a superpower in a noisy world.

principles.notes:
## Notes

Pain plus reflection equals progress. That formula alone was
worth the read. Every failed launch or botched hire is
tuition, but only if you sit down afterwards and write out
what the mistake actually was.

Treat your team like a machine you can debug. When something
breaks, don't just patch the outcome — fix the design of the
machine that produced it. That reframe changed how I run
retros.

Believability-weighted decisions beat flat democracy. The
person who has shipped the thing three times gets more
weight than the loudest voice in the room.

The work principles half drags. It's written for a
1,500-person hedge fund, not a five-person studio. Skim it,
keep the life principles close.

## Highlights

and if you're not pushing your limits, you're not

"Every time you confront something painful, you are at a

"Principles are fundamental truths that serve as the

originals.notes:
## Notes

Grant's best point: originals aren't reckless risk-takers.
They feel fear and doubt like everyone else — they just
manage it differently. Procrastination can be productive
if it gives ideas time to incubate.

"Vuja de" — seeing something familiar with fresh eyes — is
a design superpower. The best product critiques come from
people who haven't normalized the broken flow yet.

The chapter on speaking up against bad ideas without getting
fired is practical org politics. Useful when you're the
person who sees the cliff the team is walking toward.

It's pop psychology with studies attached. Cherry-pick the
ideas that match your situation; don't treat every finding
as universal law.
originals.highlights:
## Highlights

"Originals are nonconformists who move the world forward
with new ideas, values, and goals."

"It's true that the early bird gets the worm, but we can't
forget that the early worm gets caught."

"The greatest originals are the ones who fail the most,
because they're the ones who try the most."

"Being original doesn't require being first. It just means
being different and better."

"Procrastination gives you time to consider divergent
ideas that aren't your first choice."
originals.author: Adam Grant
originals.lead: How non-conformists move the world forward.

discipline-equals-freedom.notes:
## Notes

Short, blunt, and mostly right. Willink's core argument is
that discipline isn't the opposite of freedom — it's the
price of admission. Wake up early, train, do the hard thing
first, and the rest of the day gets easier.

The "default aggressive" mindset maps onto shipping: don't
wait for perfect conditions, don't over-debate, execute
with what you have and adjust in contact.

It's repetitive if you've read Extreme Ownership. Treat this
as the pocket edition — good for rereading on a bad morning
when you're negotiating with the snooze button.

The stoic framing without the philosophy lectures is the
appeal. Less Ryan Holiday, more drill instructor.
discipline-equals-freedom.highlights:
## Highlights

"Discipline equals freedom."

"Don't expect to be motivated every day to get out there

"Implement a 'prioritize and execute' mindset."

"Ego clouds and disrupts everything."

"If you want to be tougher mentally, it is simple: be
tougher. Don't meditate on it. Just be tougher."
discipline-equals-freedom.author: Jocko Willink
discipline-equals-freedom.lead: Field Manual — discipline as the path to freedom.

sapiens.notes:
## Notes

The one idea that carries the whole book: humans dominate
because we cooperate in huge numbers, and we do it through
shared fictions. Money, companies, nations, brands — none
of them exist outside our collective agreement that they
do.

That reframing is oddly practical for a designer. A brand
is a shared fiction under active construction. A startup is
a story trying to recruit enough believers — investors,
employees, users — to become self-sustaining. My job is
partly fiction engineering.

The agricultural revolution chapter is the most contrarian
bit: wheat domesticated us, trapping people in harder,
worse lives while the species thrived. A useful pattern —
technologies that win aren't necessarily the ones that make
individual lives better.

Harari overreaches in places and the second half thins out,
but as a lens for seeing institutions as stories, it
stuck.
sapiens.highlights:
## Highlights

"Large numbers of strangers can cooperate successfully by
believing in common myths."

"You could never convince a monkey to give you a banana by
promising him limitless bananas after death in monkey
heaven."

"We did not domesticate wheat. It domesticated us."

"The Agricultural Revolution was history's biggest fraud."

"Money is the most universal and most efficient system of
mutual trust ever devised."

"History is something that very few people have been doing
while everyone else was ploughing fields and carrying water
buckets."
sapiens.author: Yuval Noah Harari
sapiens.lead: A brief history of humankind — from cognitive revolution to today.

the-art-of-war.notes:
## Notes

Barely a book about war. It's about positioning: doing the
work before the confrontation so the confrontation becomes
unnecessary. The best move is the fight that never happens.

The strategy ideas map cleanly onto product work. Winning
without fighting is basically Thiel's "escape competition"
two and a half thousand years early — don't attack a strong
position, go where the opponent isn't.

Know the terrain, know yourself, know the enemy. In my
world that's user research, an honest read on your team's
actual capabilities, and competitor analysis — and most
teams skip at least one of the three.

It reads as aphorisms, so the value depends entirely on
what you bring to it. Skimmable in an evening, worth
rereading whenever a project turns political.
the-art-of-war.highlights:
## Highlights

"The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without
fighting."

"If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear
the result of a hundred battles."

"Victorious warriors win first and then go to war, while
defeated warriors go to war first and then seek to win."

"Appear weak when you are strong, and strong when you are
weak."

"Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, and when
you move, fall like a thunderbolt."

"In the midst of chaos, there is also opportunity."
the-art-of-war.author: 孙武 (Sun Tzu)
the-art-of-war.lead: Strategy and conflict — still quoted in boardrooms and beyond.

the-black-swan.notes:
## Notes

The Mediocristan vs. Extremistan split is the sharpest tool
in the book. Height lives in Mediocristan — no single
person changes the average. Wealth, book sales, and startup
outcomes live in Extremistan, where one outlier is the
whole story. Most bad forecasts come from using the wrong
map.

The turkey problem is the part I retell most: a thousand
days of being fed is overwhelming evidence the farmer loves
you, right up until Thanksgiving. Past stability is not
evidence against rupture — a lesson that applies to uptime,
clients, and careers.

The narrative fallacy hits close to home. We compress messy
randomness into clean stories after the fact, then mistake
the story for understanding. Every startup post-mortem I've
read does this.

Practical takeaway: stop trying to predict rare events and
build so they don't kill you. Barbell it — very safe on one
side, small aggressive bets on the other, nothing fragile
in the middle.
the-black-swan.highlights:
## Highlights

"History does not crawl, it jumps."

"The inability to predict outliers implies the inability to
predict the course of history."

"We are quick to forget that just being alive is an
extraordinary piece of luck, a remote event, a chance
occurrence of monstrous proportions."

"It has been more profitable for us to bind together in the
wrong direction than to be alone in the right one."

"Missing a train is only painful if you run after it!
Likewise, not matching the idea of success others expect
from you is only painful if that's what you are seeking."

"Read books are far less valuable than unread ones."
the-black-swan.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
the-black-swan.lead: We underestimate rare events with massive impact.

the-undoing-project.notes:
## Notes

Lewis tells the Kahneman and Tversky story as a love story
between two opposite minds, and it works. Danny the anxious
doubter, Amos the confident knife — the ideas came out of
the friction between them.

The science is familiar if you've read Thinking, Fast and
Slow, but seeing the heuristics born in context hits
different: judgment under uncertainty runs on stories, not
statistics, and experts are barely better than anyone else.

The undoing idea itself stuck with me most. Regret is
driven by how easily we can imagine the alternative — we
grieve the near miss more than the distant one. That
asymmetry quietly shapes a lot of decisions.

Best lesson for teams: their collaboration worked because
neither owned an idea. Every draft was joint, every credit
shared — until it wasn't, and the partnership decayed. Ego
accounting kills great pairs.

Also a reminder that great research needs slack. Tversky's
line about being a little underemployed is one I quote to
clients who schedule every hour.
the-undoing-project.highlights:
## Highlights

"A part of good science is to see what everyone else can
see but think what no one else has ever said."

"The secret to doing good research is always to be a little
underemployed. You waste years by not being able to waste
hours."

"Man is a deterministic device thrown into a probabilistic
universe."

"People predict by making up stories. People predict very
little and explain everything."

"When you are a pessimist and the bad thing happens, you
live it twice. Once when you worry about it, and the second
time when it happens."
the-undoing-project.author: Michael Lewis
the-undoing-project.lead: How Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky remade how we think about thinking.

flow.notes:
## Notes

The central claim: happiness isn't something that happens
to you, it's a state you construct by controlling your own
attention. The best moments come from voluntary struggle
toward something hard, not from relaxing.

The conditions for flow are basically a design spec:

1. Clear goals — you know what done looks like
2. Immediate feedback — you know how you're doing
3. Challenge just above skill — hard enough to demand full
   attention, not so hard it produces anxiety

I now use that list to debug my own work weeks. When a
project feels miserable, one of the three is usually
missing — most often feedback loops that are too slow.

Psychic entropy is a great name for the default state:
attention scattered across worries and inputs. Flow is the
opposite — consciousness ordered around one thing. Deep
work is just this book operationalized.
flow.highlights:
## Highlights

"The best moments in our lives are not the passive,
receptive, relaxing times... The best moments usually occur
when a person's body or mind is stretched to its limits in
a voluntary effort to accomplish something difficult and
worthwhile."

"Control of consciousness determines the quality of life."

"Enjoyment appears at the boundary between boredom and
anxiety, when the challenges are just balanced with the
person's capacity to act."

"It is not the skills we actually have that determine how
we feel but the ones we think we have."

"A person who has achieved control over psychic energy and
has invested it in consciously chosen goals cannot help but
grow into a more complex being."
flow.author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
flow.lead: Optimal experience — when challenge and skill meet in the zone.

common-sense-on-mutual-funds.notes:
## Notes

Bogle's argument is almost boring, which is the point: the
market return minus costs is all investors as a group can
earn, so the fund with the lowest costs wins over time.
Everything else is marketing.

The chapters on reversion to the mean killed any interest I
had in picking funds. Yesterday's five-star manager is
statistically most likely to be tomorrow's average one —
you're paying active fees for past luck.

What I actually took away:

1. Costs and taxes compound against you just like returns
   compound for you
2. Time in the market beats timing the market, every time
3. Simplicity is a feature — one broad index fund does the
   job
4. Ignore the noise; the industry profits from your
   activity, not your returns

It's long and repetitive, but as an operating manual for
not screwing up your savings, nothing I've read beats it.
common-sense-on-mutual-funds.highlights:
## Highlights

"Time is your friend; impulse is your enemy."

"Simplicity is the master key to financial success."

"Investing is not nearly as difficult as it looks.
Successful investing involves doing a few things right and
avoiding serious mistakes."

"The greatest enemy of a good plan is the dream of a
perfect plan."

"Rely on the ordinary virtues that intelligent, balanced
human beings have relied on for centuries: common sense,
thrift, realistic expectations, patience, and
perseverance."
common-sense-on-mutual-funds.author: John C. Bogle
common-sense-on-mutual-funds.lead: Bogle on indexing, costs, and long-term investing.

how-emotions-are-made.notes:
## Notes

This one quietly rewired how I think about people. Emotions
aren't hardwired reactions that happen to us — the brain
constructs them on the fly from bodily signals, context,
and the concepts we've learned. Anger isn't a circuit that
fires; it's a prediction.

The body-budget idea is the most practical part. The brain's
main job is regulating energy, and a lot of what we label
"emotion" is really a budget problem: bad sleep, no food,
too much cortisol. Before assuming a hard conversation is
about the conversation, check the budget.

Emotional granularity is a skill worth training. The finer
your vocabulary for what you're feeling, the more options
your brain has for responding. "Stressed" is a dead end;
"overcommitted and behind on one thing" is actionable.

For product work: users don't have fixed emotional
reactions to interfaces. Context and expectation construct
the experience, which means we have more design leverage
than we think.
how-emotions-are-made.highlights:
## Highlights

"Emotions are not reactions to the world; they are your
constructions of the world."

"You are not at the mercy of mythical emotion circuits
buried deep inside some ancient part of your brain: you
are an architect of your own experience."

"An emotion is your brain's creation of what your bodily
sensations mean, in relation to what is going on around
you in the world."

"Emotions are meaning. They explain your interoceptive
changes and corresponding affective feelings, in relation
to the situation."

"Words seed your concepts, concepts drive your predictions,
predictions regulate your body budget, and your body budget
determines how you feel."
how-emotions-are-made.author: Lisa Barrett
how-emotions-are-made.lead: The brain constructs emotion — it is not hardwired in.

hackers-amp-painters.notes:
## Notes

Graham's central claim is that hackers are makers, closer
to painters than to scientists. The implication I keep
coming back to: you learn to build software by building it
and staring at what's ugly, not by studying theory first.

The wealth chapter is the best short explanation of
startups I know. Wealth is stuff people want; money is just
how we move it around. A startup compresses forty years of
work into four by creating a lot of wealth fast.

His advice to make something people want sounds obvious
until you watch how many teams optimize everything except
that. Most of my job as a tech lead is dragging attention
back to it.

The language essays are dated in the details but right in
spirit: the tools you think in shape what you can build.
Some languages let you think thoughts the others don't.

Read it as essays, not gospel. Half the book is
provocation, but the good half has aged better than almost
anything else from 2004.
hackers-amp-painters.highlights:
## Highlights

"It's hard to do a really good job on anything you don't
think about in the shower."

"A programming language is for thinking of programs, not
for expressing programs you've already thought of."

"Wealth is stuff we want: food, clothes, houses, cars,
gadgets, travel to interesting places, and so on. You can
have wealth without having money."

"In hacking, like painting, work comes in cycles."

"The recipe for great work is: very exacting taste, plus
the ability to gratify it."
hackers-amp-painters.lead: Big ideas from the computer age — startups, hackers, and how to make things people want.
hackers-amp-painters.author: Paul Graham

the-4-hour-workweek.notes:
## Notes

Most of the lifestyle-design framing hasn't aged well, but
the operating principles underneath are still sharp. I read
this less as "escape your job" and more as "stop doing work
that doesn't matter."

The DEAL framework in practice:

1. Definition — decide what you actually want; fear-setting
   beats goal-setting
2. Elimination — 80/20 everything and go on a
   low-information diet
3. Automation — build systems and delegate outcomes, not
   tasks
4. Liberation — decouple income from location and hours

Parkinson's Law is the one I apply weekly: work expands to
fill the time you give it. Tight, artificial deadlines
produce better output than generous ones.

Being busy is not the same as being productive. Ferriss is
right that busyness is usually a way to avoid the few
uncomfortable actions that actually matter.
the-4-hour-workweek.highlights:
## Highlights

"Focus on being productive instead of busy."

"What we fear doing most is usually what we most need

"Someday is a disease that will take your dreams to the

the-4-hour-workweek.author: Timothy Ferriss
the-4-hour-workweek.lead: Design a life of mobility, automation, and selective ignorance.

switch.notes:
## Notes

The Rider-Elephant-Path model is the most useful framing of
change I've come across. The Rider is the rational planner,
the Elephant is emotion and habit, and the Path is the
environment they move through.

The playbook that stuck:

1. Direct the Rider — follow the bright spots and script
   the critical moves
2. Motivate the Elephant — shrink the change until starting
   feels easy
3. Shape the Path — tweak the environment so the right
   thing is the default

I use this constantly in product work. When users resist a
new flow, it's almost never a people problem. Clarify the
next action, make the first step tiny, or change the
interface — don't write another announcement post.
switch.highlights:
## Highlights

"What looks like resistance is often a lack of clarity."

"What looks like a people problem is often a situation
problem."

"Change is hard because people wear themselves out. And
that's the second surprise about change: What looks like
laziness is often exhaustion."

"Big problems are rarely solved with commensurately big
solutions. Instead, they are most often solved by a
sequence of small solutions."

"Knowledge does not change behavior. We have all
encountered crazy shrinks and obese doctors and divorced
marriage counselors."
switch.author: Chip Heath
switch.lead: How to change things when change is hard.

fooled-by-randomness.notes:
## Notes

The core idea: we judge decisions by outcomes, but outcomes
are mostly noise. The right way is to think in alternative
histories — a trader who got rich on one leveraged bet isn't
skilled, he's the survivor we happen to observe.

Survivorship bias is everywhere once you see it. Every
founder story I read now gets a mental asterisk: where are
the people who did exactly the same thing and blew up?

Checking numbers too often means consuming noise. The
shorter the window, the more randomness dominates the
signal. I moved my analytics review from daily to weekly
and lost nothing.

Taleb's tone gets exhausting, but the math underneath is
sound: rare events dominate outcomes, and we are wired to
underestimate them.
fooled-by-randomness.highlights:
## Highlights

"Mild success can be explainable by skills and labor. Wild
success is attributable to variance."

"It does not matter how frequently something succeeds if
failure is too costly to bear."

"Lucky fools do not bear the slightest suspicion that they
may be lucky fools."

"We favor the visible, the embedded, the personal, the
narrated, and the tangible; we scorn the abstract."

"Probability is not a mere computation of odds on the dice
or more complicated variants; it is the acceptance of the
lack of certainty in our knowledge and the development of
methods for dealing with our ignorance."
fooled-by-randomness.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
fooled-by-randomness.lead: We confuse luck with skill — especially in markets and careers.
